_note: Batch 14 — the last 116. Concepts the first hundred left out, workflow for the parts of the job that are not mixing, and mastering depth on the mix bus. Closes the bank at 1000.

questions.q: What are formants and why do they matter?
questions.short: Resonances of the vocal tract. They say how big the singer is, and pitch shifting moves them.
steps: Think of pitch as the note and formants as the size of the body producing it.
When you pitch a vocal up, the formants rise too, which implies a smaller person.
Use formant correction to shift pitch without changing implied size.
Keep shifts within 3–4 semitones where the artefacts stay hidden.
For chipmunk or deep effects, let the formants move — that is the effect.
questions.why: The vocal tract resonates at fixed frequencies regardless of the note being sung, which is how you recognise a voice across its whole range. A pitch shifter moves those resonances along with the fundamental, so the ear concludes the speaker changed size rather than pitch.
questions.watch: Formant correction on a heavily shifted vocal often sounds worse than the shift did.

questions.q: Why does tuned vocal sound artificial even on slow settings?
questions.short: It is flattening the vibrato and the slides, not just the pitch.
steps: Slow the retune speed so slides survive.
Raise the vibrato or humanise setting so held notes still move.
Correct note by note rather than running a global setting.
Leave the approach into each note uncorrected.
Tune the start of a note and release the correction on the sustain.
questions.why: Pitch correction treats deviation from a target as error, but vibrato and portamento are deliberate deviation. A setting fast enough to fix an out-of-tune note is also fast enough to remove the expression around it.
questions.watch: A perfectly tuned vocal with no vibrato sounds synthetic even when every note is right.

questions.q: Why do my edits click?
questions.short: You cut where the waveform was not at zero. The jump is the click.
steps: Put a 2–5 ms fade on every edit point.
Snap cuts to zero crossings where the DAW supports it.
Use crossfades rather than butt edits on sustained material.
Check edits at high volume on headphones; clicks hide on speakers.
If a click persists, the problem is a DC offset rather than the edit.
questions.why: A click is a discontinuity, which contains energy at every frequency. Cutting mid-waveform forces the speaker to jump instantly from one value to another, and that instantaneous step is heard as a click no matter how short the edit.
questions.watch: A fade shorter than 2 ms often does not fix it. A fade longer than 10 ms removes the attack.

questions.q: Why is the frequency axis logarithmic?
questions.short: Because pitch is. An octave is a doubling, so equal musical steps are unequal in hertz.
steps: Remember each octave doubles: 50, 100, 200, 400, 800.
An octave at the bottom is 50 Hz wide; at the top it is 10,000 Hz wide.
This is why a 100 Hz cut is drastic and a 100 Hz cut at 10 kHz is nothing.
Set Q in octaves rather than in hertz when you can.
Sweep by ear in musical intervals, not in fixed hertz steps.
questions.why: Human pitch perception is proportional rather than absolute, so doubling the frequency always sounds like one octave whether that doubling is 40 Hz or 4,000. An EQ display that spaced frequencies evenly would compress the entire bass range into a few pixels.
questions.watch: A bandwidth that is gentle at 5 kHz is surgical at 80 Hz. Same Q, very different effect.

questions.q: What does a phase rotator or all-pass filter do?
questions.short: Changes when frequencies arrive without changing their level. It can gain you headroom.
steps: Use it on asymmetric sources like voice and kick to even out the waveform.
Watch the peak meter drop with no audible change — that is the headroom gain.
Try it before reaching for a clipper on a lopsided waveform.
Every EQ filter already rotates phase; this just does it deliberately.
If you hear a difference, you have gone too far.
questions.why: Voices and kicks produce waveforms where one polarity peaks much higher than the other, so the peak meter reads the asymmetry rather than the loudness. Rotating phase redistributes those peaks and can recover a decibel or two of headroom for free.
questions.watch: It changes the waveform, so any parallel copy must get the same treatment or they will not sum.

questions.q: How do I tell a resonance from a harmonic?
questions.short: A harmonic moves with the note. A resonance stays in the same place.
steps: Play a different note and listen: if the problem frequency moves, it is harmonic.
If it stays, it is the room, the shell or the body — cut it.
Never cut a harmonic narrowly; you will thin the instrument on some notes only.
Use dynamic EQ for harmonics that only become a problem occasionally.
Sweep with a narrow boost to find it, then cut less than you boosted.
questions.why: A resonance is a property of a physical object or space, so it sits at a fixed frequency no matter what is played through it. A harmonic belongs to the note, so cutting it fixes one note and ruins the rest.
questions.watch: Narrow cuts at fixed frequencies on melodic instruments produce notes that randomly sound weak.

questions.q: Why does everything sound worse when I solo it?
questions.short: Because you mixed it to work with everything else. Solo is a diagnostic, not a goal.
steps: Use solo to find a problem, then fix it with everything playing.
Expect a good guitar to sound thin alone and a good vocal to sound bright.
Never set EQ or level in solo.
If something sounds great soloed, check whether it is too full in context.
Use mute rather than solo to judge whether an element is earning its place.
questions.why: Mixing is the allocation of a fixed amount of spectral room, so every element is deliberately incomplete to leave space for the others. A part that sounds complete alone is occupying room something else needs.
questions.watch: Players will ask why their part sounds thin soloed. It is supposed to.

questions.q: Why does my mix sound small compared to commercial records?
questions.short: Usually arrangement and low-mid buildup, not loudness. Size is contrast.
steps: Check 200–400 Hz across the whole mix; cumulative buildup kills size.
Count the simultaneous sustained parts; more than three is usually too many.
Make sure something is genuinely quiet so the loud parts have a reference.
Check your low end is mono and controlled.
Match loudness before comparing to a commercial record.
questions.why: Commercial records sound big mostly because they are arranged to leave room, not because of a processing secret. A dense mix with crowded low mids reads as loud and flat regardless of what is on the bus.
questions.watch: Comparing to an unmatched louder reference will always make your mix sound small.

questions.q: Dynamic EQ or multiband compression?
questions.short: Dynamic EQ for narrow, occasional problems. Multiband for broad, constant control.
steps: Use dynamic EQ when one frequency misbehaves sometimes — sibilance, a honky note.
Use multiband when a whole band needs consistent control — a boomy low end throughout.
Dynamic EQ is transparent at narrow settings; multiband is not.
Fewer bands is nearly always better.
If you need more than two bands, fix it at the source instead.
questions.why: Dynamic EQ changes gain in a narrow band only while a threshold is exceeded, which makes it surgical. Multiband splits the signal through crossovers that affect phase across the whole spectrum, so it is a bigger intervention for a bigger problem.
questions.watch: Multiband on a mix bus with aggressive settings is the fastest way to a lifeless master.

questions.q: Why does my bass get quieter in mono?
questions.short: Stereo content below 120 Hz partially cancels. Make the low end mono and the problem goes.
steps: Mono everything below 120 Hz.
Check for a stereo widener on the bass or the mix bus.
Check multi-mic sources for polarity problems.
Use a correlation meter to find which band is negative.
Re-check after: mono bass should be the same level as stereo bass.
questions.why: Summing to mono adds the two channels, so anything out of phase between them cancels. Low frequencies have long wavelengths and high energy, which makes the loss both large and very audible.
questions.watch: Club and phone playback are effectively mono in the low end. This is not a theoretical problem.

questions.q: Why do I need headroom if digital does not care?
questions.short: Not for noise. For the plugins and the mastering engineer.
steps: Leave 6 dB on the mix bus for whoever masters it.
Many analogue-modelling plugins expect a specific input level and change character above it.
Intersample peaks can exceed your meter after conversion.
Working quiet keeps you honest about balance rather than loudness.
Gain stage per channel rather than fixing everything at the end.
questions.why: In 24-bit the noise floor is irrelevant, so the old reason for headroom is gone. The modern reasons are that modelled plugins behave differently at different input levels, and that a master with no room left cannot be adjusted without pulling everything down first.
questions.watch: Mixing loud makes everything sound better and tells you nothing about balance.

questions.q: What are intersample peaks and should I care?
questions.short: Peaks that appear between samples after conversion. They distort on playback.
steps: Use a true-peak meter, not a sample-peak meter.
Target −1 dBTP for streaming delivery.
Expect lossy encoding to add another decibel of peak.
Enable true-peak limiting on the final limiter.
If a master reads 0 dBFS sample peak, it is almost certainly over on true peak.
questions.why: A digital file stores points, and the converter draws a smooth curve through them on playback. That curve can rise above the highest stored sample, so a file that never exceeds 0 dBFS on paper can still clip the converter.
questions.watch: Lossy codecs shift peaks. A file that is fine as WAV can clip as MP3.

questions.q: Why must I level-match when comparing?
questions.short: Louder always sounds better. Without matching, every comparison is meaningless.
steps: Match loudness before any A/B, including plugin bypass.
Use a LUFS meter rather than peak to match.
A difference of 1 dB is enough to bias the judgement.
Match before comparing your mix to a reference.
Re-match whenever you change the gain of anything in the chain.
questions.why: Loudness increases perceived bass and treble as well as level, so a louder version sounds fuller and more detailed regardless of its quality. The effect is strong enough to override trained judgement, which is why it has to be eliminated rather than allowed for.
questions.watch: Plugins with output gain are the most common unmatched comparison in a session.

questions.q: How does the ear actually locate sound?
questions.short: Level difference below, time difference above, and both matter for width.
steps: Use level panning for precise placement; it works at all frequencies.
Use small time differences for width, but check mono.
Low frequencies are hard to localise, which is why bass goes centre.
High frequencies localise most sharply, which is why hats pan well.
Reverb and early reflections tell the ear about distance, not direction.
questions.why: Below about 800 Hz the ear uses the time difference between the two ears; above that it uses level and the shadowing of the head. That is why panning a bass guitar does little while panning a shaker does a lot.
questions.watch: Time-based width cancels in mono. Level-based panning does not.

questions.q: Should my sends be pre-fader or post-fader?
questions.short: Post-fader for reverb and delay. Pre-fader only when you want the effect independent.
steps: Use post-fader for effects so the wet level follows the fader.
Use pre-fader for a parallel path you want to control separately.
Pre-fader sends still feed the effect when the fader is down — useful and surprising.
Check your DAW's default; it varies.
Automating a post-fader channel automates its reverb too, which is usually what you want.
questions.why: A post-fader send scales with the channel, so riding a vocal down takes its reverb with it and the balance stays constant. A pre-fader send ignores the fader, which means the effect stays at full level while the source disappears.
questions.watch: A forgotten pre-fader send is why a muted channel can still be audible.

questions.q: Why does my low end sound different in every room?
questions.short: Room modes. Every room reinforces and cancels different low frequencies.
steps: Check the low end on headphones as well as speakers.
Move your head a metre and listen — if the bass changes, it is the room.
Use a reference track you know well to calibrate your expectation.
Do not EQ the mix to fix a room problem.
Treat the room if you can; bass traps in corners do the most.
questions.why: A room's dimensions create standing waves at specific low frequencies, which are much louder at some positions and nearly absent at others. The microphone of your ear is in one of those positions, so the bass you hear is partly the room.
questions.watch: EQing to fix a room mode makes the mix wrong everywhere else.

questions.q: Does a fast attack always kill the transient?
questions.short: No. A fast attack with a fast release can increase perceived punch.
steps: Try a fast attack with a fast release and listen — it can add aggression.
A slow attack lets the transient through and compresses the body.
A fast attack with a slow release flattens everything; that is the dull setting.
Judge by ear and by the gain-reduction meter's movement.
Match loudness before deciding which sounds punchier.
questions.why: Punch is the difference between the peak and the body that follows it, and a fast release restores gain quickly enough to let the body swell back up. The usual advice assumes a slow release, where the same fast attack does flatten everything.
questions.watch: Fast attack and fast release can distort low-frequency sources. Watch the bass.

questions.q: Why use two compressors instead of one?
questions.short: Each works less, so each artefact is smaller. Three decibels twice beats six once.
steps: First compressor slow and gentle for overall level.
Second faster for the peaks that slip through.
Keep each under 4 dB of gain reduction.
Use different characters — opto then FET is the classic pairing.
If one is doing all the work, the split is not helping.
questions.why: Compression artefacts scale with how hard a compressor is working, so splitting the job halves the distortion and pumping from each stage. The total reduction is the same but the audible cost is far lower.
questions.watch: Two compressors badly set sound worse than one well set. It is not automatic.

questions.q: Should EQ come before or after compression on a bus?
questions.short: Subtractive before, additive after. The compressor should not react to what you are removing.
steps: Put corrective cuts before the compressor.
Put tonal boosts after, so they are not squashed.
A high-pass before bus compression stops the low end driving the gain reduction.
Try both orders and listen; on a bus the difference is audible.
Keep the moves small either way.
questions.why: A compressor responds to total energy, so a boost before it increases gain reduction and the compressor then removes most of what you added. Cutting first means the compressor reacts to the signal you intend rather than the problem you are fixing.
questions.watch: On a mix bus the low end dominates the compressor unless you filter the sidechain.

questions.q: What does glue actually mean?
questions.short: Shared movement. One compressor making everything duck together is what the ear reads as one record.
steps: Use one compressor across the whole mix, 1.5:1 to 2:1, 1–3 dB.
Set the release to the tempo so it breathes with the song.
Insert it early and mix into it rather than adding it at the end.
High-pass the sidechain so the kick does not drive everything.
Bypass occasionally; if the mix falls apart, it is doing too much.
questions.why: When one compressor controls everything, a loud snare momentarily ducks the guitars and the vocal too. That shared movement is a cue the ear uses to decide several sources share one space, which is the whole effect.
questions.watch: Adding bus compression at the end invalidates every balance decision made under it.

questions.q: What is the difference between parallel and serial processing?
questions.short: Serial changes the signal. Parallel adds a changed copy alongside the original.
steps: Use parallel when you want an extreme effect without losing the original.
Use serial when the change should apply to everything.
Check phase: a parallel path with EQ or a different latency will cancel.
Blend the parallel path in until you hear it, then back off.
Mute the dry path to hear what you are actually blending in.
questions.why: Parallel processing preserves the original dynamics underneath while adding density on top, which is why a heavily compressed parallel copy sounds powerful where the same compression in series sounds crushed.
questions.watch: Any EQ or plugin latency in a parallel path can cancel the low end. Null-test it.

questions.q: What exactly is a transient?
questions.short: The first few milliseconds. It carries almost all the information about what hit what.
steps: Think of it as the attack before the pitch becomes clear.
Protect it on percussive sources; it is what makes them identifiable.
Slow compressor attacks let it through; fast ones reduce it.
A transient shaper changes it directly without affecting level.
Removing transients is how you make something sit back without lowering it.
questions.why: The ear identifies a sound source largely from its onset, which is why a piano with its attack removed sounds like a flute. That makes the first few milliseconds disproportionately important compared to the sustain that follows.
questions.watch: Transients cost headroom out of proportion to their loudness. That is the trade.

questions.q: What is a limiter actually taking away?
questions.short: The transients, and the difference between loud and quiet. That is what loudness costs.
steps: Watch the gain reduction; more than 3–4 dB regularly is heavy.
Listen to the drums; they lose attack first.
Compare at matched loudness to hear what was removed.
Use a clipper for brief peaks so the limiter works less.
Decide how much loudness is worth the dynamics, then stop.
questions.why: A limiter can only create loudness by reducing the peaks, and the peaks are the transients. The record gets louder because the quiet parts move closer to the loud ones, which is precisely the contrast that made it feel powerful.
questions.watch: Streaming normalises loudness back down, so heavy limiting loses the dynamics for nothing.

questions.q: Why does my mix fall apart on other systems?
questions.short: You mixed to your room's faults. Check on three systems and fix what all three agree on.
steps: Check on monitors, headphones and a phone.
Fix only problems that appear on all three.
If one system disagrees, it is probably that system.
Use a reference track on each to calibrate your expectation.
Treat the room before buying better speakers.
questions.why: Every monitoring setup has a response you compensate for without realising, so a mix is partly a mirror of the room's faults. Agreement across different systems is what separates a real problem from a local one.
questions.watch: Three systems that all flatter the same band will all mislead you the same way.

questions.q: When should I reach for mid/side?
questions.short: When you need to treat the centre and the sides differently. Rarely, and gently.
steps: Use it to clean the centre of a two-track you cannot separate.
Use it to high-pass the sides while keeping the centre full.
Use it to add air to the sides only.
Check mono after every mid/side move.
Keep the moves under 2 dB on a mix bus.
questions.why: Mid/side decomposes a stereo signal into what is common and what differs between channels, which maps usefully onto lead elements and ambience. It is powerful precisely because it cuts across the normal channel structure, which is also why it breaks mono compatibility so easily.
questions.watch: Boosting the sides reduces the mono signal. Always check the sum.

questions.q: What actually makes a vocal sit in a mix?
questions.short: Consistency first, then space for it. Level is the last thing to try.
steps: Compress for consistency so every word is present.
Carve 1–4 kHz on whatever is masking it, not on the vocal.
Give it a depth cue — a short delay rather than a long reverb.
Ride the fader by phrase rather than setting one level.
Only then adjust the overall level.
questions.why: A vocal that disappears is usually intermittently masked rather than uniformly quiet, which is why raising it makes the loud words too loud before the quiet ones become audible. Consistency and carving fix the actual mechanism.
questions.watch: A vocal loud enough to never be masked is almost always too loud.

questions.q: How much of mixing is really arrangement?
questions.short: Most of it. If two parts occupy the same space, one of them should stop.
steps: Before EQing a clash, ask whether both parts need to play there.
Mute each element for a section and see if anything is lost.
Move a part up or down an octave rather than carving it.
Change when a part plays rather than how it sounds.
If a fix needs more than three EQ moves, it is an arrangement problem.
questions.why: A mix distributes a fixed amount of spectral and temporal room, and no processing creates more. When two parts want the same space, removal or relocation is the only solution that leaves both sounding like themselves.
questions.watch: Arrangement changes need the artist's agreement. Raise them early, not at the end.

questions.q: Why does saturation make bass audible on small speakers?
questions.short: It creates harmonics higher up, and the ear reconstructs the missing fundamental from them.
steps: Saturate the bass until the note is audible with the sub removed.
Check on a laptop or phone speaker, not on monitors.
Use parallel saturation to keep the clean low end intact.
Target 200 Hz–1 kHz for the harmonics that small speakers reproduce.
Do not raise the sub to compensate; it will not help.
questions.why: The ear infers a fundamental from the spacing of its harmonics, so a 50 Hz note is heard even when the speaker reproduces nothing below 300 Hz, as long as the harmonics are present. Saturation generates exactly those harmonics.
questions.watch: Too much saturation makes the bass audible and unpleasant. Stop at audible.

questions.q: Why high-pass a compressor's sidechain?
questions.short: So the kick stops controlling the gain of everything else.
steps: High-pass the sidechain at 80–120 Hz on bus and mix compressors.
Listen to the gain reduction meter; it should stop following the kick.
Use it whenever a compressor pumps in time with the bass.
It changes what the compressor hears, not what you hear.
Most modern compressors have it built in.
questions.why: Low frequencies carry far more energy than high ones, so a compressor reacting to the full signal is mostly reacting to the kick and bass. Filtering the detector lets it respond to the whole mix rather than to its loudest component.
questions.watch: Filtering too high makes the compressor ignore the body of the mix.

questions.q: What do headphones get wrong?
questions.short: Width and low end. No crossfeed, and no room to load the bass.
steps: Check width on speakers; headphones exaggerate separation.
Check low end on speakers or against a reference you know.
Use headphones for detail, editing and sibilance.
Take breaks; headphone fatigue arrives faster.
If you only have headphones, reference constantly.
questions.why: Headphones deliver each channel to one ear with no acoustic crossfeed, so panned material sits inside the head rather than in front of you. The low end is also reproduced without room reinforcement, so it reads differently from any speaker.
questions.watch: Headphone-only mixes usually come out too wide and too light in the bass.

questions.q: When does oversampling actually matter?
questions.short: Whenever a plugin distorts. Saturation, clipping and hard limiting all alias without it.
steps: Turn it on for saturation, distortion, clippers and limiters.
Leave it off for EQ and compression that is not generating harmonics.
Listen to high-pitched material; aliasing is most obvious there.
Expect higher CPU and some added latency.
Oversample at mixdown even if you worked without it.
questions.why: Distortion creates harmonics above the original signal, and any that exceed half the sample rate fold back down into the audible range as inharmonic tones. Oversampling moves that ceiling up so the harmonics have room before folding.
questions.watch: Aliasing sounds like harshness rather than distortion, which is why it goes unnoticed.

questions.q: What actually makes drums punch?
questions.short: The contrast between attack and the space after it. Punch is a difference, not a level.
steps: Keep the transient intact with a slower compressor attack.
Shorten the decay so there is space after the hit.
Make sure nothing sustained is filling the gap between hits.
Check the kick and bass are not masking each other's attack.
Raise the attack with a transient designer rather than compressing harder.
questions.why: Punch is perceived as the jump from near-silence to peak, so it depends on what surrounds the hit as much as on the hit itself. A sustained pad across the gaps removes the contrast and the drums stop punching however loud they are.
questions.watch: Louder drums in a dense mix feel less punchy, not more.

questions.q: Why does my balance change when I turn it up?
questions.short: Your ears change with level. Mix at one moderate volume and check at others.
steps: Pick a moderate reference level and do most of the work there.
Check quietly — the balance of the important elements shows up best.
Check loud briefly for low end, then go back.
Never make tonal decisions at high volume.
Use a meter to return to the same level each session.
questions.why: Hearing sensitivity to bass and treble rises faster with level than it does for mids, so a mix balanced loud will sound thin and mid-heavy quiet. The balance did not change; your ears did.
questions.watch: If it works quietly it usually works loud. The reverse is not true.

questions.q: What should I fix first in a bad mix?
questions.short: Low end, then vocal, then everything else. In that order, every time.
steps: Get the kick and bass relationship right before anything else.
Then make the lead vocal consistently audible.
Then the snare and the main rhythmic elements.
Then everything else, which is mostly carving.
Leave effects and width until the balance works dry.
questions.why: Low end consumes most of the headroom and the vocal carries most of the meaning, so both change every other decision in the mix. Fixing them last means redoing everything that was balanced against the broken version.
questions.watch: Starting with reverb and width means rebalancing after every structural fix.

questions.q: What is wrong with presets?
questions.short: Nothing, as a starting point. They were made for a different recording.
steps: Use a preset to get into the right area quickly.
Immediately check whether its moves make sense for your source.
Reset anything you cannot justify.
Pay attention to input level; many presets assume a specific one.
Build your own from the presets you keep adjusting the same way.
questions.why: A preset encodes decisions about a signal that is not yours, so its EQ moves target resonances your recording may not have. It is useful as a shortcut to a starting character and misleading as a destination.
questions.watch: A vocal preset on a dark voice usually makes it darker, not brighter.

questions.q: When is distortion a feature rather than a fault?
questions.short: When it adds harmonics you want. Fault is when it adds ones you did not choose.
steps: Use saturation deliberately for density and for small-speaker translation.
Avoid clipping converters and plugin inputs; that distortion is uncontrolled.
Oversample anything generating harmonics.
Check the result on a small speaker, where harmonics matter most.
If you cannot hear it but the meter moved, you probably want less.
questions.why: All saturation is distortion, and the difference between a desirable and an undesirable version is whether the harmonics are musically related and controlled. Converter clipping produces unrelated high-order harmonics, which is why it sounds harsh rather than warm.
questions.watch: Accidental distortion in a recording cannot be removed. Catch it at the source.

questions.q: How loud should the lead vocal be?
questions.short: Loud enough to follow the words at low volume. Check quietly, not loudly.
steps: Turn the monitors down until the mix is barely audible.
The vocal should still be followable; if not, it is too quiet.
Check against a reference in the same genre at matched loudness.
Different genres sit the vocal very differently — match the tradition.
Ride it rather than finding one correct number.
questions.why: At low playback levels the ear's reduced bass and treble sensitivity strips the mix back to its midrange core, which is where the vocal lives. That makes quiet listening the most reliable test of whether the vocal is carrying the song.
questions.watch: Genres differ enormously. A gospel vocal sits higher than a house vocal.

questions.q: What can a null test tell me?
questions.short: Whether two signals are genuinely identical. It is the only way to be certain.
steps: Duplicate a track, flip polarity on one, and listen — silence means identical.
Use it to check whether a plugin is actually doing anything.
Use it to verify a parallel path is phase-aligned.
Use it to find what changed between two mix versions.
Any residual is the difference, and you can listen to it.
questions.why: Summing a signal with its own polarity-inverted copy cancels everything they share, leaving only what differs. That makes it an objective test in a field where almost everything else is a judgement.
questions.watch: A tiny timing or gain difference will prevent a null even when nothing meaningful changed.

questions.q: How many plugins should be on a channel?
questions.short: As few as fix the problem. If you cannot say what one is doing, remove it.
steps: Bypass each plugin and listen; keep only what you miss.
Fix a problem once rather than with three gentle versions of the same move.
Reach for the source or the arrangement before a fourth plugin.
Watch cumulative latency and phase shift across a long chain.
A finished vocal often needs four or five, not fifteen.
questions.why: Every plugin adds some phase shift, some latency and some colouration, and those accumulate whether or not any individual one is audible. A long chain of small moves usually produces less control and more damage than a short chain of decisive ones.
questions.watch: Bypassing the whole chain and preferring it is a common and useful shock.

questions.q: Does the song's key affect mixing decisions?
questions.short: Yes. Resonances and low-end problems land on the key's notes.
steps: Tune the kick and 808 to the root or fifth.
Expect the muddiest frequency to relate to the key, not a fixed number.
Watch for one note in the bass line that is always too loud — that is a room mode or a resonance.
Use dynamic EQ for note-dependent problems rather than static cuts.
Check a key change for new problem frequencies.
questions.why: A mix's low-end energy is concentrated on the notes being played, so a song in F has its buildup at F and its octaves. A fixed EQ cut that works for one song can be in the wrong place for the next.
questions.watch: A static low-mid cut that works on every song is probably too wide to be doing much.

questions.q: Why do my stems not sum to the same mix?
questions.short: Bus processing. Anything on the master is not in the stems unless you put it there.
steps: Print stems through the mix bus chain, or supply it separately.
Check the summed stems null against the mix before sending.
Include any sidechain relationships that cross stem boundaries.
Print all stems from the same start point with the same length.
Say clearly whether the stems include master processing.
questions.why: Mix bus compression responds to the whole mix, so applying it to each stem separately gives a different result than applying it once to the sum. Omitting it entirely gives yet another. Neither matches unless it is handled deliberately.
questions.watch: A mastering engineer receiving stems that do not sum to your mix will produce a different record.

questions.q: What makes a mix sound expensive?
questions.short: Control and contrast. Nothing surprising, nothing fighting, and real dynamics between sections.
steps: Make sure nothing jumps out unintentionally — that is control.
Make sure the sections genuinely differ in density.
Clean the low mids; buildup is the clearest amateur signature.
Keep the lead consistently intelligible.
Remove rather than add when in doubt.
questions.why: Expensive-sounding records are usually the result of a hundred small decisions to remove things, not of expensive processing. What a listener hears as polish is the absence of problems rather than the presence of effects.
questions.watch: Chasing a sound with plugins when the arrangement is crowded never works.

questions.q: How do I know when my ears are gone?
questions.short: When you start adding top end. That is the first symptom, every time.
steps: Stop if you find yourself brightening everything.
Take ten minutes away every hour.
Mix at moderate levels; loud monitoring fatigues faster.
Make the important decisions in the first two hours.
Check the next morning before sending anything.
questions.why: Sustained exposure temporarily reduces sensitivity at high frequencies, so a mix that sounded right an hour ago now sounds dull. The natural response is to add treble, which is why fatigued mixes are consistently too bright the next day.
questions.watch: Fatigue feels like the mix got worse, not like your hearing changed.

questions.q: How do I mix a genre I do not know?
questions.short: Reference heavily and ask what the genre's priority is. Every genre ranks elements differently.
steps: Find three current reference records in that exact sub-style.
Identify what sits loudest; it varies enormously between genres.
Ask the artist what matters most to them in the arrangement.
Match the low-end balance before anything else; it differs most.
Resist applying your usual genre's conventions.
questions.why: Genres differ less in processing than in hierarchy — which element is allowed to dominate, how loud the vocal sits, how much low end is normal. Those are conventions you cannot deduce from the multitrack.
questions.watch: A technically good mix that ignores the genre's conventions will be rejected.

questions.q: What can mastering not fix?
questions.short: Balance, masking and arrangement. Mastering works on the whole, not on parts.
steps: Fix a buried vocal in the mix; mastering cannot raise it alone.
Fix a clashing kick and bass in the mix.
Fix distortion and noise in the mix or the recording.
Send a mix you are happy with, not one you hope will be rescued.
Ask for a revision rather than expecting mastering to compensate.
questions.why: Mastering applies broad processing to a stereo file, so every move affects everything at once. Raising 3 kHz to help a vocal also raises it on the snare, the guitars and the cymbals, which is why balance problems have to be solved upstream.
questions.watch: A mastering engineer who says the mix needs work is usually right.

questions.q: Where does a clipper belong in the chain?
questions.short: Before the limiter, and on percussive sources. Small amounts in several places.
steps: Clip individual drums 1–2 dB before they reach the bus.
Clip the mix bus 1–2 dB before the limiter.
Keep each stage small; several gentle clips beat one hard one.
Listen on sustained material for distortion.
Oversample the clipper.
questions.why: Clipping removes only the samples above the ceiling, so it costs nothing on a short transient and everything on a sustained tone. Spreading small amounts across the chain means no single stage distorts audibly while the total peak reduction is substantial.
questions.watch: Clipping the mix bus hard destroys the stereo image before it sounds distorted.

questions.q: What should I ask before starting a mix?
questions.short: References, priorities, and what they do not want. Five minutes saves five revisions.
steps: Ask for two or three reference records.
Ask what the most important element is to them.
Ask what they dislike about the rough mix.
Ask where it will be heard — club, radio, streaming, church.
Agree how many revisions are included before you start.
questions.why: Most revision rounds come from unstated expectations rather than technical faults. A reference record communicates more about a desired sound in thirty seconds than a conversation does in an hour.
questions.watch: An artist who cannot name a reference usually cannot name what is wrong either.

questions.q: Should I listen to the artist's rough mix?
questions.short: Yes, once, carefully. It tells you what they have been living with.
steps: Listen once before opening the session.
Note the balance choices, especially the vocal level.
Note anything deliberately strange; it is probably intentional.
Then put it away and mix properly.
Compare at the end to check you did not lose something they loved.
questions.why: The artist has heard the rough hundreds of times, so it defines their expectation of the song regardless of its technical quality. Diverging from it without knowing you are diverging is the most common cause of a rejected mix.
questions.watch: Copying the rough's faults is as bad as ignoring its intentions.

questions.q: How much setup should I do before mixing?
questions.short: Enough that you never hunt for a track. Twenty minutes, then do not touch it again.
steps: Name and colour every track consistently.
Route to buses: drums, bass, vocals, music, effects.
Set a rough balance before inserting a single plugin.
Clean the edits and remove empty tracks.
Save as a template point you can return to.
questions.why: Mixing is a long sequence of small comparisons, and anything that interrupts that flow costs more than the time it takes. Setup is cheap when it is done once and expensive when it is done repeatedly mid-decision.
questions.watch: Over-organising is procrastination. Twenty minutes, not two hours.

questions.q: Can I mix properly on a laptop?
questions.short: Yes, if you reference constantly and check the low end elsewhere.
steps: Use decent headphones and learn their response with reference tracks.
Check the low end on anything with real bass before committing.
Use a reference track in every session, matched for loudness.
Check on a phone speaker for the opposite extreme.
Treat laptop speakers as a mono midrange check, which is genuinely useful.
questions.why: The limitation of a laptop setup is not resolution but the absence of reliable low-frequency information. Referencing substitutes external knowledge for what the system cannot tell you, which is why it matters more here than anywhere else.
questions.watch: Laptop speakers reproduce almost nothing below 300 Hz. Never judge bass there.

questions.q: How many mix revisions are reasonable?
questions.short: Two or three, agreed in advance. Unlimited revisions serve nobody.
steps: Agree the number before you start, in writing.
Ask for all notes at once rather than one at a time.
Group small notes into a single pass.
Charge for revisions caused by new recordings or arrangement changes.
If round three is still about the same thing, talk rather than mix.
questions.why: Revision rounds beyond the third are usually a symptom of unclear expectations rather than remaining technical problems. Agreeing a limit forces the conversation that would have prevented them.
questions.watch: Free unlimited revisions trains clients to send notes instead of thinking.

questions.q: What do I do when the recording is simply bad?
questions.short: Say so early, fix what is fixable, and be honest about the ceiling.
steps: Tell the client before you spend hours, not after.
Fix noise, timing and tuning first; those respond to work.
Accept that distortion and room are usually permanent.
Suggest re-recording the one element that matters most.
Set expectations in writing so the final mix is not a surprise.
questions.why: Some faults are additive and removable while others are baked into the waveform. Knowing which is which before starting determines whether the session is a mix or a salvage operation, and the client needs to know too.
questions.watch: Spending ten hours rescuing a take nobody will re-record helps no one.

questions.q: What mic placement decisions matter most?
questions.short: Distance sets the tone, angle sets the brightness. Both beat any EQ afterwards.
steps: Move the mic before reaching for EQ; a few inches changes more than a filter.
Closer gives more low end through proximity effect and less room.
Off-axis reduces brightness and sibilance.
Point the mic at the part of the instrument you want to hear.
Listen on headphones while someone moves the mic.
questions.why: Microphone position changes the acoustic balance before the signal exists, so it alters the ratio of direct to reflected sound and the instrument's own radiation pattern. No EQ can reconstruct a balance that was never captured.
questions.watch: The proximity effect makes close positions bass-heavy. That is a choice, not a fault.

questions.q: How do I record a decent vocal at home?
questions.short: Get close, kill the reflections behind the mic, and watch your levels.
steps: Sing close, 15–20 cm, to raise the direct-to-room ratio.
Put absorption behind the microphone, not behind the singer.
Aim for peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS; do not record hot.
Face into the room rather than into a corner.
Use a pop filter and keep it a hand's width from the mic.
questions.why: An untreated room's problem is reflected energy arriving shortly after the direct sound. Getting closer increases the direct level without increasing the reflections, which improves the ratio more effectively than any treatment you can afford.
questions.watch: Close miking adds proximity bass and plosives. High-pass and use the pop filter.

questions.q: How do I check phase while recording?
questions.short: Flip polarity and keep the fuller version. Do it before the take, not after.
steps: With two mics up, flip polarity on one and listen to the low end.
Keep whichever sounds fuller.
Move one mic a few centimetres and listen again.
Apply the three-to-one rule: second mic three times as far as the first is from the source.
Check in mono, where cancellation is most obvious.
questions.why: Two mics at different distances receive the same sound at different times, which cancels some frequencies and reinforces others. Fixing it while the mics are still up costs seconds; fixing it afterwards is approximate at best.
questions.watch: The fuller option is usually right, but check the whole range, not just the bass.

questions.q: How do I comp a vocal without it sounding assembled?
questions.short: Cut on breaths and keep whole phrases. Switching mid-word is what gives it away.
steps: Cut at breaths wherever possible.
Prefer whole phrases from one take over word-by-word assembly.
Crossfade every join, 5–20 ms.
Match the level either side of each join before fading.
Listen through once for joins only, with no other processing.
questions.why: Tone and room sound vary slightly between takes, and the ear detects that change most easily in the middle of a sustained sound. Breaths mask the transition because they contain no pitch to compare.
questions.watch: A comp that is perfect in solo can reveal its joins once compression raises the gaps.

questions.q: Should I print effects or keep them live?
questions.short: Print when the decision is made and the CPU matters. Always keep an unprinted copy.
steps: Print heavy processing once you are sure, to save CPU.
Keep a muted copy of the unprocessed track in the session.
Name printed tracks clearly so future-you knows what is baked in.
Do not print anything the client might ask to change.
Print before sending to anyone else's system.
questions.why: Printing trades flexibility for stability and performance. Keeping the source alongside means the trade is reversible, which is the only way printing is safe on a project that is not finished.
questions.watch: Printed effects that are wrong are expensive. Keep the original every time.

questions.q: How do I keep a session from becoming unmanageable?
questions.short: Delete what you are not using. A hidden muted track is still a decision you have to re-make.
steps: Delete rather than mute tracks you have rejected.
Consolidate alternative takes into a clearly named folder.
Keep one version of each element active.
Save incrementally with meaningful names.
Clean up before you stop, not when you return.
questions.why: Every muted track is an unresolved decision that costs attention each time you scroll past it. Sessions get slow to work in long before they get slow to run.
questions.watch: Delete only after the project is backed up. Then delete confidently.

questions.q: How do I mix well when I have no time?
questions.short: Balance, low end, vocal. Stop there. Those three carry most of the result.
steps: Spend the first third of your time on static balance alone.
Fix the kick and bass relationship next.
Make the vocal consistent and clearly audible.
Add effects only where the song obviously needs them.
Do not start anything you cannot finish.
questions.why: Most of a mix's perceived quality comes from balance, low-end control and vocal clarity, and all three are achievable quickly. Detail work has steeply diminishing returns, which makes it the right thing to cut when time is short.
questions.watch: Half-finished automation is worse than none. Finish or do not start.

questions.q: How should I back up a project?
questions.short: Three copies, two media, one off-site. Audio is not recoverable from nothing.
steps: Keep the working copy, a local backup and a cloud or off-site copy.
Back up after every session, not at the end of the project.
Include the audio files, not just the session file.
Test a restore occasionally; an untested backup is a guess.
Archive finished projects with their plugin list.
questions.why: Recorded audio is unique in a way that documents are not — a lost vocal take cannot be reconstructed from memory or from anyone else's copy. The cost of redundancy is trivial against the cost of a single loss.
questions.watch: A backup on the same drive as the original is not a backup.

questions.q: What should I send a client with the final mix?
questions.short: A clearly named WAV, an MP3 for phones, and a note on what changed.
steps: Send a 24-bit WAV at the session sample rate for mastering.
Send an MP3 too; most clients will listen on a phone.
Name files with artist, title, version and date.
Write two lines on what changed since the last version.
Say explicitly whether the file is mastered or not.
questions.why: Most client confusion comes from not knowing which file is current or whether it is finished. A clear name and two lines of context prevent more revision rounds than any technical improvement.
questions.watch: A client comparing an unmastered mix to a mastered reference will always prefer the reference.

questions.q: What alternate versions should I print?
questions.short: Instrumental, TV mix, a cappella and clean. Print them while the session is open.
steps: Print an instrumental with no lead vocal.
Print a TV mix with backgrounds but no lead.
Print an a cappella of the vocals alone.
Print a clean version if there is explicit language.
Print them all at the same time, from the same mix.
questions.why: Alternate versions are nearly free while the session is open and expensive to recreate later, because plugin versions, licences and settings drift. Printing them at delivery is insurance against a request that always arrives eventually.
questions.watch: A TV mix printed months later rarely matches the original exactly.

questions.q: How do I get useful feedback on a mix?
questions.short: Ask specific questions. Can you hear every word is a better question than what do you think.
steps: Ask whether the words are clear, not whether they like it.
Ask them to listen on their normal system, not yours.
Ask for timestamps on anything that bothers them.
Ignore notes about level that are really about arrangement.
Collect all notes before changing anything.
questions.why: Untrained listeners describe symptoms rather than causes, so open questions produce vague answers. Specific questions give answers you can act on and reveal the real problem more reliably than technical discussion.
questions.watch: The vocal is too quiet often means the vocal is not clear. Check before raising it.

questions.q: How do I mix my own music objectively?
questions.short: Add time and distance. You cannot hear your own mix fresh on the day you made it.
steps: Leave at least a day between mixing and deciding.
Reference against records you did not make.
Get one outside opinion before finalising.
Mix on a different system than you produced on.
Write down what you intend before you start, then check against it.
questions.why: Familiarity with the arrangement lets you hear parts that are not actually audible, because memory fills them in. That makes self-mixing systematically biased toward under-mixing the elements you know best.
questions.watch: You will defend decisions you made as a producer. Separate the two roles deliberately.

questions.q: What belongs in a mix template?
questions.short: Routing and sends, not processing. A template with plugins pre-loaded makes every song sound the same.
steps: Include buses, sends and naming conventions.
Include two or three reverbs and a delay on sends.
Do not include channel EQ or compression.
Include a reference track slot and a metering chain.
Update it when you find yourself doing the same setup twice.
questions.why: A template should remove setup, not decisions. Pre-loaded processing applies choices made for a different song before you have heard this one, which is how engineers end up with a signature sound they did not intend.
questions.watch: A template with a vocal chain pre-loaded means every vocal gets the same treatment.

questions.q: Should I recall an old mix or start again?
questions.short: Recall for small changes, restart for big ones. Restarting is faster than it sounds.
steps: Recall if the notes are level and balance changes.
Restart if the arrangement changed or the notes are about character.
Keep the old mix as a reference while restarting.
Check plugin versions before assuming a recall will match.
Print the old mix before touching anything.
questions.why: A recalled session carries every decision made under the old assumptions, so fundamental changes mean fighting your own previous work. Starting fresh with the old mix as a reference is often quicker and almost always better.
questions.watch: Plugin updates can change a recalled mix. Print before you update anything.

questions.q: Do I need different masters for different platforms?
questions.short: Usually one. Master around −14 LUFS and let normalisation handle the rest.
steps: Master once to around −14 LUFS integrated, −1 dBTP.
Make a louder master only for club or CD delivery.
Do not make a separate master per streaming service.
Check true peak for lossy encoding headroom.
Keep the dynamics; normalisation removes the benefit of loudness.
questions.why: Streaming platforms normalise to similar targets, so a single master at a sensible loudness plays back correctly everywhere. Making a louder version for one service gains nothing after normalisation and loses dynamics permanently.
questions.watch: Club and broadcast genuinely differ. Streaming services mostly do not.

questions.q: How do I work with a producer who keeps changing the arrangement?
questions.short: Freeze the arrangement before mixing. Mixing a moving target wastes everyone's time.
steps: Agree the arrangement is final before you start.
Ask for a bounce of the agreed arrangement as the reference.
Treat arrangement changes as a new mix, not a revision.
Keep a rough balance going while the arrangement is still moving.
Say clearly what a change costs in time.
questions.why: Every balance and automation decision is made against a specific arrangement, so adding or removing a part invalidates a proportion of the work. The cost is invisible to the person requesting it, which is why it has to be stated.
questions.watch: Mixing while the arrangement moves teaches the collaborator that changes are free.

questions.q: What do I do if I cannot treat my room?
questions.short: Use headphones for the low end and reference constantly. Position matters more than gear.
steps: Set up symmetrically and avoid sitting against a wall.
Use headphones to check anything below 150 Hz.
Reference a track you know in every session.
Put something absorbent at the first reflection points, even a duvet.
Learn your room's lie rather than trying to fix it.
questions.why: Room problems are mostly low-frequency and mostly positional, so moving the listening position often helps more than treatment you can afford. What cannot be fixed can be worked around with a second reference system.
questions.watch: Buying better monitors for an untreated room mostly reveals the room more clearly.

questions.q: Should I reuse the same vocal chain on every song?
questions.short: Reuse the structure, not the settings. Same order, different numbers.
steps: Keep the plugin order consistent so you work quickly.
Reset the settings for every new voice.
Keep the de-esser frequency per singer; it varies a lot.
Note the settings that worked for each singer you work with often.
Bypass the whole chain at the end and check it is helping.
questions.why: The order of operations is a general principle that holds across voices, while the settings depend on the specific recording. Reusing both produces a signature sound rather than a good mix of this song.
questions.watch: A chain that works on every voice is probably doing very little on most of them.

questions.q: When is a mix ready for mastering?
questions.short: When you would release it as is. Mastering improves a good mix; it does not finish one.
steps: Leave 6 dB of headroom and no limiter on the bus.
Check it on three systems first.
Make sure the vocal and low end are right; those cannot be fixed later.
Send 24-bit WAV at the session sample rate.
Include references and a note on anything deliberate.
questions.why: Mastering applies broad moves to a finished balance, so any problem that needs an individual element changed must be solved first. Sending a mix you hope will be rescued guarantees disappointment.
questions.watch: Removing your bus limiter changes the balance. Mix without it, not with it then off.

questions.q: How do I deal with plugin latency?
questions.short: Trust delay compensation for playback, but check parallel paths manually.
steps: Leave delay compensation on for mixing.
Check any parallel path with a null test.
Disable linear-phase and lookahead plugins while recording.
Freeze or print high-latency chains if monitoring suffers.
Verify the final bounce against what you heard.
questions.why: Delay compensation aligns tracks at the output, but a parallel copy with a different chain can still be offset by a few samples, which cancels the low end. The DAW does not warn you because it believes everything is aligned.
questions.watch: External hardware inserts are not automatically compensated. Measure them.

questions.q: How do I decide what to charge for a mix?
questions.short: Per song, with revisions defined. Hourly punishes you for getting faster.
steps: Quote per song, not per hour.
State how many revisions are included.
Charge separately for editing, tuning and arrangement work.
Raise rates when you are consistently busy, not when you feel ready.
Get half up front for new clients.
questions.why: Hourly billing means your income falls as your skill rises, since experience makes you faster at the same result. Per-song pricing aligns what you earn with what the client receives.
questions.watch: Undefined revisions turn a fixed price into unlimited work.

questions.q: Why does my mix sound dull after mastering?
questions.short: The limiter removed the transients that carried the brightness.
steps: Reduce the limiting; more than 3–4 dB regularly costs top end.
Clip the drum transients before the limiter so it works less.
Check for a multiband compressor squashing the high band.
Compare at matched loudness before concluding it is dull.
Add brightness in the mix rather than on the master.
questions.why: Transients contain most of the high-frequency energy, so a limiter reducing peaks is disproportionately reducing treble. The master measures brighter on a meter and sounds duller, because the sustained content was never the problem.
questions.watch: Adding a high shelf to compensate makes the sustained parts harsh without restoring the attack.

questions.q: How do I match my mix to a reference?
questions.short: Match the broad balance in three bands, not the curve. Match loudness first.
steps: Match loudness before comparing anything.
Compare low, mid and high in broad terms rather than frequency by frequency.
Fix differences in the mix, not with a bus EQ.
Use two or three references, not one.
Accept that arrangement differences cannot be matched with EQ.
questions.why: A reference's spectral curve reflects its arrangement as much as its processing, so matching the curve exactly imposes another song's instrumentation on yours. Broad balance transfers; detail does not.
questions.watch: Automatic matching plugins copy the arrangement's fingerprint, not its quality.

questions.q: How do I control the low end on the mix bus?
questions.short: Mostly in the mix, not on the bus. On the bus, filter the compressor's sidechain.
steps: Fix kick and bass balance in the mix before touching the bus.
High-pass the bus compressor's sidechain at 80–120 Hz.
Mono everything below 120 Hz.
Use a gentle high-pass at 25–30 Hz to remove inaudible rumble.
Use multiband on the low band only if nothing else worked.
questions.why: Low frequencies carry most of the energy, so they dominate every bus processor unless deliberately excluded. Controlling them at source preserves the detail that bus-level compression and EQ inevitably blur.
questions.watch: Multiband on the low end is the fastest way to lose the groove between kick and bass.

questions.q: How do I check the stereo width of a master?
questions.short: Fold to mono and listen for anything that disappears. The meter is secondary.
steps: Fold to mono and check nothing important vanishes.
Check the correlation meter stays mostly positive.
Verify the low end is mono below 120 Hz.
Listen on headphones and on a single speaker.
Narrow rather than widen if anything is uncertain.
questions.why: A correlation meter reports the overall relationship between channels and can read acceptably while one specific element cancels completely. Only listening in mono finds that element.
questions.watch: Clubs, phones and many PA systems are effectively mono. This is not optional.

questions.q: How much limiting is too much?
questions.short: When the drums stop moving. Watch the gain reduction and listen to the kick.
steps: Keep regular gain reduction under 3–4 dB.
Listen to the kick and snare; they lose attack first.
Compare at matched loudness with the limiter bypassed.
Use a clipper before the limiter to reduce the work it does.
Stop when more loudness stops making it sound better.
questions.why: A limiter's damage is concentrated on transients, so percussion degrades long before sustained material shows any sign. The kick losing its attack is the earliest reliable indicator, and it happens before most people notice anything wrong.
questions.watch: Streaming normalisation removes the benefit. The damage stays.

questions.q: Does every mix need mastering?
questions.short: Every release needs the loudness and format work. Not every release needs another engineer.
steps: If releasing commercially, get a second pair of ears if the budget allows.
If self-mastering, do it on another day and on another system.
At minimum set loudness, true peak and fades correctly.
Check sequence and spacing if it is an album.
Never master on the same monitoring you mixed on if you can avoid it.
questions.why: Mastering does two separable jobs: technical preparation for delivery, and an outside judgement on the mix. The first is mandatory and learnable; the second is valuable precisely because it comes from someone who has not heard the song two hundred times.
questions.watch: Self-mastering immediately after mixing provides neither distance nor a second opinion.

questions.q: How do I set fades and spacing on a release?
questions.short: Fade where the music says, and leave 1–3 seconds between tracks depending on energy.
steps: Start the fade where the music naturally settles, not at a fixed time.
Leave a short fade at the end of every track to avoid a click.
Space energetic transitions closer, 1–2 seconds.
Space reflective transitions wider, 2–4 seconds.
Listen to each transition in context, not in isolation.
questions.why: Gaps between tracks carry meaning in sequence, since the pause after a loud song is part of how the next one lands. A uniform gap applied mechanically flattens the dynamics of the record as a whole.
questions.watch: A hard stop with no fade clicks on some players even if it looks clean.

questions.q: What do I check before releasing a master?
questions.short: Mono, true peak, loudness, start and end, and a listen all the way through.
steps: Listen start to finish without stopping, once.
Check mono compatibility.
Verify true peak is at or below −1 dBTP.
Check loudness is near the target for the platform.
Check there is no click at the start or the end and no silence missing.
questions.why: Most released faults are not subtle processing errors but mechanical ones — a click, a truncated ending, a peak over. They survive because nobody listened to the final file in full after the last change.
questions.watch: Always check the exact file you are uploading, not the one before the last render.

questions.q: What should actually be on my mix bus?
questions.short: Very little. Gentle compression, a decibel of EQ, maybe saturation. Nothing else.
steps: One compressor at 1.5:1 to 2:1 doing 1–3 dB.
Broad EQ moves of a decibel or less.
Optional saturation, driven until just audible.
No limiter while mixing if someone else will master.
Insert everything early and mix into it, not at the end.
questions.why: Every bus move applies to forty channels at once, which is why a decibel there is equivalent to a decibel on everything. Heavy bus processing is almost always compensating for a balance problem that would be cheaper to fix at source.
questions.watch: A mix that collapses when the bus chain is bypassed was never balanced.

questions.q: Why does my master sound small on a phone?
questions.short: Everything you can hear is below what a phone reproduces. Build the midrange.
steps: Saturate the bass so its harmonics carry the note above 300 Hz.
Check 200 Hz–2 kHz is not scooped; phones live there.
Make sure the vocal is clear in the midrange, not just present overall.
Check the mix in mono; phone speakers are a single driver.
Test on an actual phone at arm's length, not on a simulation.
questions.why: A phone speaker reproduces almost nothing below 300 Hz and has very little output in the low mids, so a mix whose weight lives there arrives hollow. The midrange has to carry the whole record on that device.
questions.watch: A mix built to sound big on a phone can sound mid-heavy on speakers. Check both.

questions.q: How do I make an album sound like one record?
questions.short: Same room, same chain, same references, and check them back to back at the end.
steps: Mix them in the same room on the same monitoring.
Use the same bus chain across every song.
Use the same references for all of them.
Listen to all the transitions back to back before finalising.
Adjust the outliers to the group rather than perfecting each alone.
questions.why: Consistency is judged in comparison rather than in isolation, so songs mixed weeks apart drift even when each is good. The back-to-back listen is the only way to hear what a listener playing the record will hear.
questions.watch: Perfecting each song separately reliably produces an inconsistent album.

questions.q: The client says it is not loud enough. What now?
aliases: not as loud as other songs
questions.short: Show them a level-matched comparison first. Usually it is not loudness they are hearing.
steps: Play your mix and their reference at matched loudness.
If yours still sounds smaller, the problem is balance or arrangement.
Check the low mids and the vocal level before adding limiting.
Explain streaming normalisation — louder masters get turned down.
If they still want it louder, do it, and keep the dynamic version.
questions.why: Perceived loudness comes from density and midrange energy as much as from level, so a well-balanced mix can sound louder than a more limited one at the same measurement. The request is usually about impact rather than volume.
questions.watch: Winning this argument with measurements rarely works. Demonstrate it instead.

questions.q: Why is the top end of my mix crowded?
questions.short: Cymbals, sibilance and air boosts all stacking. De-ess the sources, not the bus.
steps: De-ess every vocal individually before touching the bus.
Low-pass the cymbals and hats at 14–16 kHz.
Remove air-band boosts from more than two sources.
Use dynamic EQ at 6–10 kHz on the bus for the remaining peaks.
Check each source's contribution by muting.
questions.why: Air-band boosts are cumulative and individually inaudible, so five sources each lifted 2 dB produce a harsh top end nobody can trace to one track. Fixing it on the bus dulls the sources that were not contributing.
questions.watch: A dull-sounding bus fix usually means the problem was two sources, not all of them.

questions.q: Do analogue emulations on the bus actually help?
questions.short: Sometimes, in small amounts. Most of the effect is the level change they introduce.
steps: Match loudness before deciding whether it improved anything.
Use one, not a chain of three.
Watch the input level; many change character with drive.
Check for added noise, which some add deliberately.
If you cannot hear it at matched loudness, remove it.
questions.why: These plugins add harmonic distortion and small frequency shifts, both of which are real but subtle. Their reputation comes partly from the output level increase many apply by default, which is why level matching changes the verdict so often.
questions.watch: Stacking three emulations compounds noise and phase shift for very little gain.

questions.q: Should I print the mix in real time or render offline?
questions.short: Offline is fine and usually identical. Listen to the result either way.
steps: Render offline unless you have external hardware in the chain.
Always listen to the rendered file, not just the session.
Check the start and end for truncation.
Null the render against a real-time print if you are unsure.
Render at the session sample rate and 24-bit.
questions.why: Modern offline rendering is sample-accurate for in-the-box chains, so the old advice to always print in real time is mostly obsolete. The exception is anything involving external hardware or a plugin whose behaviour depends on real-time input.
questions.watch: Some plugins with randomness or modulation render differently each time. Null-test them.

questions.q: Why does my mix sound flat and two-dimensional?
questions.short: Everything is equally dry and equally loud. Depth needs some things further away.
steps: Keep the lead vocal and kick dry and forward.
Push two or three elements genuinely back with reverb and a 2–4 kHz cut.
Use pre-delay on the close elements and none on the distant ones.
Vary the amount of space between sections.
Reduce the high end on the distant elements.
questions.why: Depth is relative, so it requires contrast between near and far. When every source gets the same reverb send they all sit at the same distance, and the mix reads as a flat wall regardless of how wide it is.
questions.watch: Adding reverb to everything to create depth achieves the opposite.

questions.q: Why do sections of my song sound like different mixes?
questions.short: The bus compressor is reacting differently to different densities. Check its movement per section.
steps: Watch the bus compressor's gain reduction across the whole song.
If it varies by more than 2 dB between sections, ease the ratio or threshold.
Automate the bus compressor's threshold per section if needed.
Check the low end is not driving the difference; filter the sidechain.
Compare the sections back to back at matched loudness.
questions.why: A bus compressor responds to total energy, so a dense chorus drives far more gain reduction than a sparse verse. That changes the tonal balance between sections even though no setting changed.
questions.watch: A chorus that gets quieter as it gets fuller is the classic sign of this.
